definition: A lookup table mapping discrete IDs (tokens, users, items) to dense trainable vectors.
details: A lookup table mapping discrete IDs (tokens, users, items) to dense trainable vectors. The first layer of every language model; the output projection is sometimes tied to it (weight tying) to save parameters.

explainer.lead: An embedding layer turns discrete IDs, such as token or user IDs, into numerical vectors that a neural network can process. Its vectors are learned during training, and the layer is the first stop for input tokens in a language model.

tiers.eli5: Think of a wall of numbered pigeonholes, one for each word, user, or item. Each pigeonhole holds a short list of numbers, and the network uses that list instead of the ID. During training, those numbers are adjusted so they become more useful for the task.
tiers.practitioner: Configure the table with vocabulary size V and embedding dimension d, then feed it integer IDs to retrieve dense vectors for the rest of the network. Its V × d parameters can make memory usage substantial for large vocabularies. In language models, output-projection weights can optionally be tied to the embedding weights to reduce the parameter count.
tiers.paperLevel: For V discrete IDs and embedding dimension d, the layer stores a trainable matrix E in R^(V × d); the representation of ID i is e_i = E[i]. The table therefore has Vd parameters, so its storage grows with both vocabulary size and dimension. Weight tying optionally reuses E in the output projection instead of maintaining a separate projection matrix.

explainer.example: Suppose the token "cat" has ID 42 in a model using three-dimensional embeddings. The layer selects row 42 of its table, which might be [0.2, -0.7, 1.1], and sends that vector to the next layer.

usedIn.name: Language models
usedIn.detail: The embedding layer maps input token IDs to vectors as the model's first layer.

usedIn.name: Recommender systems
usedIn.detail: User and item IDs can be mapped to trainable vectors for subsequent processing.

explainer.intuition: An ID is only a label, not a useful numerical input. An embedding layer gives each ID its own learned vector, allowing the network to work with tokens, users, or items as continuous representations.
howItWorks: Assign every token, user, or item a discrete integer ID.
Create a table with one dense vector, or row, for each possible ID.
For each input ID, retrieve its corresponding row from the table.
Pass the retrieved vector to the next part of the neural network.
Update the vectors during training; in some language models, also reuse the table for the output projection.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a simple trainable bridge between discrete symbols and the continuous computations of neural networks. Weight tying can also reduce parameters by sharing this table with a language model's output projection.
misconceptions: An embedding vector is not the ID itself converted into a number; it is a separate trainable row with a chosen dimension.
Weight tying is optional, not a requirement of every embedding layer.

diagram.caption: IDs select trainable vectors from the embedding table; a language model may also tie its output projection to that table.
